rv.q: Twenty years have done something wonderful to McCraney's play. It now feels more like an assured masterpiece than the first work of a prodigy; here, polished to a deep lustre, is the finest exertion of McCraney's talents, elevated by a cast with staggering gifts.
The superlative direction further establishes the many levels on which the play moves.
It’s somehow both tight and spacious, a structure with its own integrity that still makes room for all the galvanizing possibilities of play.
The production is often beautiful to witness, yet at times its stark style prevents the show and its characters from feeling tangible.
The Brothers Size remains filled with urgency, reaffirming McCraney’s place in the American theatrical landscape and reminding us why his voice first demanded attention.
And in a new production co-directed by Bijan Sheibani and Mr. McCraney, these issues are addressed with a grace and grit that do full justice to the text.

In The Shed’s intimate staging, The Brothers Size lets the audience in on the title family’s tough reality of whether to live in the dreams of their past or wake up to their fraught realities, with mythic and indelible results.
It’s the ‘how’ of McCraney’s art that elevates the tropes into a poetic symphony of near-tragedy and spiritual release.
The entire production is worth more than the price of admission.
Running only ninety minutes, this highly concentrated drama achieves a power that eludes so many contemporary plays.
There is power and beauty in this revival, thanks to McCraney’s ear for dialogue, the subtle change in our perception of the characters and their relationships...
For all its beauty and occasional flashes of humor, “The Brothers Size” remains more evocative than fully satisfying.
In this stellar revival, the performances and production match the writer's clarity.
This 20th-anniversary production of the show makes a strong argument for its place in the canon of great American plays.
There’s a simple elegance to the storytelling, enhanced by shifts into poetic language heightened by Spencer Doughtie’s lighting cues.

The Brothers Size is worthy of an esteemed place in the pantheon of such classic plays about siblings as Suzan-Lori Parks’s Topdog/Underdog, Sam Shepard’s True West, and August Wilson’s The Piano Lesson, a powerful, gripping, timeless tale of freedom and brotherhood.

cn.t: Critics celebrate McCraney's powerful drama as scorching, electric, and robust, praising its poetic fusion of Yoruba mythology with contemporary Black life. Holland's performance and the production's balletic physicality earn particular acclaim in this welcome revival.

vr.q: I would highly recommend this production, especially if you haven't seen the play before.
if you haven't seen any of his plays on stage before I really would not recommend missing this one
